questions.title: Does “certifying” under La. Rev. Stat. § 9:3550(G)(3)(a) require a human signature, or can an unsigned corporate statement suffice?
questions.question_body: The panel holds that the statute does not explicitly require a signature and reads “certifying” as permitting an unsigned corporate certification transmitted by email. I’m confused because Benitez noted lack of a signature among the defects (though it didn’t say that alone was dispositive). Under Louisiana interpretive canons and the strict-compliance line of cases (Eaglin, Delatte, Britten), how do we reconcile the idea of strict adherence with allowing an unsigned, non-identifying corporate certification? Would Louisiana courts likely demand some authenticated, attributable act (e.g., e-signature, named affiant) to qualify as “certifying,” or is the Fifth Circuit’s reading consistent with Louisiana practice for corporate certifications generally?

questions.title: What counts as “receipt” by the insurer when cancellation notices are delivered electronically under § 9:3550(G)(3)(b)(i)?
questions.question_body: The court accepts Black’s definitions and concludes GoAuto had “receipt” once its web service accepted the APAC email and triggered automatic cancellation, even though no human at GoAuto handled the request until later. Under Louisiana law, is machine-level intake sufficient to constitute “receipt,” particularly given the strict-compliance requirement intended to fix the exact time of cancellation? Are there Louisiana cases or administrative practices that treat server acceptance or API calls as legal receipt for statutory notice, or is the Fifth Circuit making an Erie prediction in a novel context?

questions.title: How did strict-compliance doctrine apply to the sequence problem: cancellation before later-added signature stamp?
questions.question_body: Plaintiffs argued the certification lacked a signature when the policy auto-cancelled, and only later did an APAC employee add a signature stamp to printed documents. Given Louisiana’s strict-compliance rule, does the timing mismatch matter if the statute does not require a signature at all? More broadly, under Louisiana cancellation cases, do later-curative steps (like post-cancellation stamping) ever validate an earlier defective cancellation, or is compliance measured strictly at the moment the insurer acts on the cancellation request?

questions.title: Was the district court’s “private carrier” rationale for receipt/delivery legally tenable under § 9:3550, and what would it have meant if the Fifth Circuit hadn’t relied on email?
questions.question_body: The district court apparently treated the APAC employee who physically delivered documents to GoAuto as a “private carrier,” analogizing to a railroad case. The Fifth Circuit called that imaginative and unnecessary to reach. As a matter of Louisiana statutory interpretation, is “private carrier” in § 9:3550(G)(3)(a) meant to describe the method of sending from the finance company to the insurer (like FedEx/UPS), or could it reasonably encompass in-house or related-entity couriers? If email hadn’t sufficed, would the private-carrier theory likely fail because of control/agency concerns between APAC and GoAuto?

questions.title: How does compliance with § 9:3550 foreclose the plaintiffs’ misrepresentation and good-faith claims against the insurer?
questions.question_body: The court affirms summary judgment on all claims after finding statutory compliance. For Louisiana bad faith and misrepresentation theories tied to cancellation (e.g., asserting coverage ended when it hadn’t), is statutory effectiveness of cancellation dispositive as a matter of law, or could there still be separate tort or contractual duties breached by the way cancellation was communicated? What is the Louisiana standard linking statutory compliance with the absence of insurer bad faith in premium-financing cancellation disputes?

questions.title: Why did the Fifth Circuit decline to certify the statutory-interpretation questions to the Louisiana Supreme Court despite unsettled terms?
questions.question_body: The court emphasizes a general reluctance to certify absent a compelling reason and says mere absence of a state high court definition isn’t enough. Given that Louisiana’s strict-compliance doctrine and the undefined statutory terms (“certifying,” “receipt”) could have system-wide implications, what factors typically persuade the Fifth Circuit to certify, and why didn’t those apply here? Is this effectively an Erie guess about Louisiana law on electronic receipt and corporate certification, and how would a contrary future Louisiana Supreme Court interpretation affect cancellations that occurred under this ruling?

questions.title: What standard of review and summary-judgment framework governed the panel’s resolution, and did any factual disputes preclude summary judgment?
questions.question_body: The parties filed cross-motions focused solely on statutory compliance. The opinion reads like de novo review of statutory interpretation applied to undisputed facts about GoAuto/APAC systems. Were there any genuine disputes of material fact (e.g., about when the email hit GoAuto’s system, custody of the repository, or which entity’s employee stamped documents) that should have gone to a jury under federal summary-judgment standards? How does the Fifth Circuit treat such mixed questions (fact about receipt mechanics; law about what counts as receipt) in diversity cases applying Louisiana law?
